title: Hedyotis corymbosa: Spotting and Controlling Diamond Flower in Rice
metaTitle: Hedyotis corymbosa in Rice: How to Spot and Control It
metaDescription: Hedyotis corymbosa, or diamond flower, is a thin leaved broadleaf weed in lowland rice. See how to spot it and keep it from seeding in your palay.
excerpt: Hedyotis corymbosa, also called diamond flower, is a slender broadleaf weed with long, narrow leaves. It grows in irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. There, farmers call it pisak or dalumbang. This page shows you how to spot it and how it competes with your palay. Then you will learn how to control it before it sets seed.

blocks.text:
Hedyotis corymbosa is a small annual herb in the coffee family, Rubiaceae. In English it is called diamond flower. Its thin stems branch out, and the plant either stands upright or spreads along the ground. Local names include dalumbang, kaddok na kalinga, palarapdap, pisak and pisek. Farmers also use these names for its cousin, Hedyotis biflora.

Look for it in irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields. This weed lives for only one season. Within one crop, it sprouts, flowers, sets seed and dies. Seeds are its only way to spread. The tiny seeds drop near the mother plant and stay in the soil until the next planting. So a few plants left alone this season can turn into a thick stand next time.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about Hedyotis corymbosa
rows: Dalumbang, kaddok na kalinga,palarapdap, pisak, pisek
Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: Check the low spaces between rice hills for a slender herb with thin, branched stems. Its leaves are long and narrow, and they taper slowly to a point at the tip. The leaves look narrow, yet this is a broadleaf weed, not a grass or sedge. Instead of a leaf sheath wrapped around the stem, it has leaves set in pairs on a freely branching stem. Tiny flowers sit in small umbrella like clusters of 2 to 8.

items: Long, narrow leaves that slowly taper to a fine point at the tip.
Thin, branched stems standing upright or sprawling low between the rice hills.
Leaves set in pairs along the stem, with no sheath wrapping the stem.
Tiny flowers in small umbrella like clusters of 2 to 8.
Look alike tip: Hedyotis biflora shares its local names but has oval to oblong leaves.

blocks.text:
This weed looks harmless, but it still competes with your palay. It draws water and nutrients from the same soil where your rice roots feed. It also takes a share of the fertilizer you pay for. When many plants sprout together, they fill the gaps between rice hills while the crop is young and weak.

Because it is an annual that spreads only by seed, each plant that flowers adds more seed to your soil. As a result, the weed returns with every new crop. Its seeds can also mix with the harvested palay. Thick patches give insects a place to hide close to your rice too.

items: Walk the paddy while the rice is young and pull these slender plants early. Their thin leaves are easy to miss among rice seedlings.
Remove plants before the tiny flower clusters set seed. Each seed you stop now is one less weed next season.
Keep water in the paddy after planting where your field allows. Small seeded annual weeds sprout more easily on exposed soil than under water.
Clean the bunds too. Plants growing on the pilapil can drop seed back into the field.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold Hedyotis corymbosa down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows the PhilRice eDamuhan recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Hedyotis corymbosa Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Hedyotis corymbosa?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. You can also put the weeding days on your [cropping calendar](/features/cropping-calendar), so the team knows when to go in.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Hedyotis corymbosa

items.q: What is Hedyotis corymbosa called in the Philippines?
items.a: Farmers use several local names for it. You may hear dalumbang, kaddok na kalinga, palarapdap, pisak or pisek. In English it is called diamond flower. These same local names also cover Hedyotis biflora, a close cousin. If you need to tell them apart, check the leaves. This one has long, narrow leaves that taper to a point.

items.q: How do I control diamond flower in my rice field?
items.a: Start with clean binhi and good land preparation, then keep proper water in the paddy. Pull young plants by hand before they flower. If many come up, use a herbicide for broadleaf weeds that fits the age of your rice. Always read and follow the FPA registered label on the product.

items.q: Why do I see more of it every season?
items.a: Each plant you miss drops tiny seeds that stay in the soil. When you plant again, many of those seeds sprout with the new crop. So the patch grows a little thicker each time. Pull the plants before they flower, and clean the bunds as well, so fewer seeds go back into the soil.
